VIDEO.title: Romans 11 Is a Warning Christians Keep Ignoring
VIDEO.series: The Book of Romans, Every Word (playlist of 28 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Romans 11:11-36 · Episode 19 (#19 of 28 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher opens with a sentence argued over for centuries: 'All Israel will be saved' (11:26). Whatever Paul says here, he is not merely explaining Israel's future; he is exposing something dangerous in us. He reads Romans 11:11-36: Israel stumbled but did not fall; Gentiles are grafted into the olive tree and must not boast; a partial hardening lasts until the fullness of the Gentiles; then the doxology (11:33-36).

Recap of Romans 9-11: God's word has not failed, because covenant membership was never defined by ethnicity but by promise and mercy (9). Israel's problem is not lack of zeal or revelation but refusal to submit to God's righteousness in Messiah, the telos of Torah (10). Now Paul shows Israel's resistance is neither total nor final.

Observations: Israel has stumbled (9:32-33), not fallen, despite killing the prophets, hardening, stupor and blindness (11:3-9). Paul argues lesser to greater four times (11:12, 15, 21, 24). He uses mirroring and inverted patterns throughout Romans 9-11, like an hourglass with smaller hourglasses inside; the teacher avoids calling them chiasms because scholars debate them. The center of the olive tree section is 11:20-22: do not be haughty, but fear.

Who is the first piece of dough and the root (11:16)? Scholars suggest the patriarchs, the Messiah, God, or early Jewish Christians. With Dwight Pryor the teacher holds it is the patriarchal covenant beginning with Abraham, so the olive tree is the historical covenant people of God, not merely 'the church'. Unbelieving branches were broken off (compare John 15:6); believing Gentiles are grafted in.

'All Israel' (11:26): the third-person pronouns of 11:28 point back to unbelieving Israel. The most natural reading, in the teacher's view, is a future turning of ethnic Israel to Jesus as Messiah; how and when is unclear. The thread is mercy: 'God has shut up all in disobedience so that He may show mercy to all' (11:32).

Old Testament background: Deuteronomy 32:21 and Isaiah 10:21-22; first fruits from Numbers 15:18-21; the olive tree from Psalm 52:8, Jeremiah 11:16 and Hosea 14:6; the nations in Isaiah 2:2, 49:6 and 56:7; a composite of Isaiah 59:20-21 and 27:9 with echoes of Jeremiah 31:33-34; mercy from Deuteronomy 30, Psalms 14 and 53, Hosea 2:23; the doxology from 1 Chronicles 29:11-14, Isaiah 40:13 and Job 41:11. Paul writes as a prophet would (Acts 22:18, 21).
The lesson: 'God's covenant promises, not human appearances, are the proper lens for interpreting both history as well as the present moment.'
QUOTES: God's covenant promises, not human appearances, are the proper lens for interpreting both history as well as the present moment.
What appears to be collapse is actually the means of expansion.
If this were a musical number, this particular passage would be the crescendo.
What looked like the defeat of a blasphemous rabbi was the greatest moment in all of human history.

method.p: Mark the four 'how much more' arguments in Romans 11:12, 15, 21 and 24. For each, write the lesser and the greater. Then draw the olive tree: root, natural branches, broken branches, grafted branches.

src.text: I say then, did they stumble so as to fall? May it never be! But by their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles, to make them jealous.

lines.text: Paul already said Israel stumbled over the stumbling stone (9:32-33). Even after 11:3-10 (prophets killed, hardened, a spirit of stupor, a snare), he says they have only stumbled, suggesting recovery. God used their stumbling to bring salvation to the Gentiles, and the jealousy motif comes from Deuteronomy 32:21.

left.text: Now if their transgression is riches for the world and their failure is riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their fullness be!

right.text: For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?

lines.text: Qal vahomer, arguing from the lesser to the greater: explicit in 11:12, structural in 11:15, implicit in 11:21 ('if God did not spare the natural branches') and explicit again in 11:24. Paul is concluding his vindication of God's character: 'this particular passage would be the crescendo.'

left.text: A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. / For though your people, O Israel, may be like the sand of the sea, / Only a remnant within them will return;

right.text: So I will make them jealous with those who are not a people; / I will provoke them to anger with a wickedly foolish nation,

lines.text: Paul already quoted these at the end of Romans 9 and 10 (9:27-28; 10:19). He reuses them to double down on the overarching purpose of Romans 9-11: God's covenant faithfulness in light of Israel's unbelief.

left.text: Of the first of your dough you shall raise up a cake as a contribution offering; as the contribution offering of the threshing floor, so you shall raise it up. From the first of your dough you shall give to Yahweh a contribution offering throughout your generations.

right.text: And if the first piece of dough is holy, the lump is also; and if the root is holy, the branches are too.

lines.text: The first fruits were understood to consecrate the whole batch. Paul applies this to the patriarchs: the people who come from them keep a covenantal consecration. This is not automatic salvation; it is covenant status that can be forfeited through unbelief. As Romans 9:6 put it, 'they are not all Israel who are descended from Israel' (Romans 9:6).

left.text: Yahweh called your name,“A green olive tree, beautiful in fruit and form”; / With the noise of a great tumult / He has kindled fire on it, / And its foliage has an evil demise.

right.text: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a partaker with them of the rich root of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you do boast against them, remember that it is not you who supports the root, but the root supports you.

lines.text: Paul draws the olive tree from the prophets (Jeremiah 11:16; Hosea 14:6). The tree is God's covenant people throughout history, rooted in Abraham. Unbelieving branches are broken off, as Jesus warned: 'If anyone does not abide in Me, he is thrown away as a branch and dries up' (John 15:6).
The center of the section: 'They were broken off for their unbelief, but you stand by your faith. Do not be haughty, but fear' (Romans 11:20).

left.text: He says, “It is too small a thing that You should be My Servant / To raise up the tribes of Jacob and to cause the preserved ones of Israel to return; / I will also give You as a light of the nations / So that My salvation may reach to the end of the earth.”

right.text: Even those I will bring to My holy mountain / And make them glad in My house of prayer. / Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be acceptable on My altar; / For My house will be called a house of prayer for all the peoples.”

lines.text: Grafting Gentiles into God's covenant people was always intended: 'all the nations will stream to it' (Isaiah 2:2). With Pryor, the teacher says believers today are grafted into Israel's covenant life, 'part of the commonwealth of Israel'.

Study note (added): Gentiles were once 'alienated from the citizenship of Israel'; 'But now in Christ Jesus you who formerly were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ' (Ephesians 2:12-13).

src.text: For I do not want you, brothers, to be uninformed of this mystery—so that you will not be wise in your own estimation—that a partial hardening has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in; and so all Israel will be saved;

lines.text: In 11:28 'they' are 'enemies for your sake' and 'beloved for the sake of the fathers': the pronouns point back to unbelieving Israel. The teacher expects a future turning of ethnic Israel to Jesus; how and when is unclear. They are beloved because of what God has done through Israel (9:4-5), not because unbelieving Israel is saved.

left.text: “A Redeemer will come to Zion, / And to those who turn from transgression in Jacob,” declares Yahweh.

right.text: “The Deliverer will come from Zion, / He will remove ungodliness from Jacob.” “And this is My covenant with them, / When I take away their sins.”

lines.text: Paul blends Isaiah 59:20-21 and 27:9, language close to the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:33-34. He changes 'to Zion' to 'from Zion'. Why? The teacher invites viewers to infer it themselves.

left.text: Who has encompassed the Spirit of Yahweh, / Or as His counselor has informed Him?

right.text: “Who has given to Me that I should repay him? / Whatever is under the whole heaven is Mine.

lines.text: 'For God has shut up all in disobedience so that He may show mercy to all' (Romans 11:32). The mercy section echoes Deuteronomy 30, Psalms 14 and 53, and Hosea 2:23. The doxology (11:33-36) draws on 1 Chronicles 29:11-14, a temple doxology, with Isaiah 40:13 and Job 41:11.

TERMS.def: Arguing from the lesser to the greater ('how much more'), used four times in 11:12-24.
The first portion offered to God, consecrating the whole (Numbers 15:18-21; Romans 11:16).
In the video, God's historical covenant people, rooted in the patriarchs.
Something once hidden, now revealed: the partial hardening of Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles (11:25).
An inverted, mirrored structure (A B B' A'). The video prefers 'inversion and mirroring' because scholars debate chiasms here.
A hymn of praise to God's glory (11:33-36).

BACKGROUND.p: Olive trees were among the most important crops of the land (Deuteronomy 8:8). Growers normally graft a cultivated shoot onto a wild stock; Paul pictures the reverse, a wild shoot grafted into a cultivated tree, which he himself calls 'contrary to nature' (11:24).
Numbers 15:17-21 commands a cake from the first of the dough to be given to Yahweh throughout Israel's generations. The first portion offered to God marked the whole as belonging to Him.
The three chapters open with Paul's grief over Israel (9:1-5) and close with praise (11:33-36). The video sees the whole section as a defense of God's covenant faithfulness, ending in doxology.

DEBATES.p: The patriarchs (the video, with Pryor; Chrysostom), the Messiah, God himself, or the first Jewish Christians. The video sets out all four before choosing the patriarchal covenant.

A future large-scale turning of ethnic Israel (the video's view), the full number of the elect remnant through history, or the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile. The pronouns in 11:28 are central to the video's argument.
Some scholars find chiastic structures in Romans 9-11; others doubt them. The video speaks of inversion, mirroring and parallelism instead.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video lists Psalm 52:8 among places 'where Israel is actually like literally called an olive tree'; there the psalmist says 'as for me, I am like a green olive tree.' Jeremiah 11:16 and Hosea 14:6 do picture Israel.
The video introduces the 'mystery' as 'verse 26'; the warning and the mystery are 11:25, and 'all Israel will be saved' is 11:26.
The captions spell the scholar 'Dwight Prior' and the argument 'kalva'; the name is Dwight Pryor and the term is qal vahomer.
The video's Jeremiah 11:16 adds 'The Lord of Hosts, who planted you, has decreed disaster against you'; that is Jeremiah 11:17.

QUESTIONS: Why does it matter whether the olive tree is 'the church' or God's covenant people through history?
What does 'do not be haughty, but fear' (11:20) look like in practice?
How can unbelieving Israel be both 'enemies' and 'beloved' (11:28)?
Where are you reading the present moment by appearances rather than by God's promises?
Which line of the doxology (11:33-36) do you need to pray this week?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: How often do we read the present moment by what we see rather than by what God has promised? The Pharisees saw Sabbath-breakers; the Lord of the Sabbath stood before them (Matthew 12). Israel feared Goliath's appearance; David came in the name of Yahweh of hosts (1 Samuel 17). The cross looked like the defeat of a blasphemous rabbi. The teacher urges reading three books well: God's word, reality and mankind, interpreting the last two through the first. A dream that sent him to God's word led his family into a painful wilderness season, and Wise Disciple emerged; this channel, Every Word, began from Jesus' answer to the devil in Matthew 4, quoting Deuteronomy 8:3.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): name one situation that looks like collapse to you right now. Write beside it one promise of God that speaks to it, and read Romans 11:33-36 aloud over it.

   Isaiah (Isaiah 56:7, LSB): "Even those I will bring to My holy mountain / And make them glad in My house of prayer. / Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be acceptable on My altar; / For My house will be called a house of prayer for all the peoples.”"
   (video) Grafting Gentiles into God's covenant people was always intended: 'all the nations will stream to it' (Isaiah 2:2). With Pryor, the teacher says believers today are grafted into Israel's covenant life, 'part of the commonwealth of Israel'. (Isaiah 2:2)
   [Background] Study note (added): Gentiles were once 'alienated from the citizenship of Israel'; 'But now in Christ Jesus you who formerly were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ' (Ephesians 2:12-13). (Ephesians 2:12-13)

## The mystery and the doxology
1. Romans 11:25-28: All Israel will be saved
   A mystery Romans 11:25-26: "For I do not want you, brothers, to be uninformed of this mystery—so that you will not be wise in your own estimation—that a partial hardening has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in; and so all Israel will be saved;" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+11:25-26
   (video) In 11:28 'they' are 'enemies for your sake' and 'beloved for the sake of the fathers': the pronouns point back to unbelieving Israel. The teacher expects a future turning of ethnic Israel to Jesus; how and when is unclear. They are beloved because of what God has done through Israel (9:4-5), not because unbelieving Israel is saved. (Romans 11:28; Romans 9:4-5)
2. Isaiah 59:20-21; 27:9; Jeremiah 31:33-34: From Zion
   Isaiah (Isaiah 59:20, LSB): "“A Redeemer will come to Zion, / And to those who turn from transgression in Jacob,” declares Yahweh."
   Paul (Romans 11:26-27, LSB): "“The Deliverer will come from Zion, / He will remove ungodliness from Jacob.” “And this is My covenant with them, / When I take away their sins.”"
   (video) Paul blends Isaiah 59:20-21 and 27:9, language close to the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:33-34. He changes 'to Zion' to 'from Zion'. Why? The teacher invites viewers to infer it themselves. (Isaiah 27:9; Jeremiah 31:33-34)
3. Romans 11:32-36; Isaiah 40:13; Job 41:11: Mercy on all
   Isaiah (Isaiah 40:13, LSB): "Who has encompassed the Spirit of Yahweh, / Or as His counselor has informed Him?"
   Job (Job 41:11, LSB): "“Who has given to Me that I should repay him? / Whatever is under the whole heaven is Mine."
   (video) 'For God has shut up all in disobedience so that He may show mercy to all' (Romans 11:32). The mercy section echoes Deuteronomy 30, Psalms 14 and 53, and Hosea 2:23. The doxology (11:33-36) draws on 1 Chronicles 29:11-14, a temple doxology, with Isaiah 40:13 and Job 41:11. (Romans 11:32; Hosea 2:23; 1 Chronicles 29:11)

## Key people
- Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: The patriarchs: in the teacher's view, the first fruits and root of the olive tree (11:16). [Background] Israel is 'beloved for the sake of the fathers' (11:28).
- Dwight Pryor: The teacher agrees with him that the dough and root are the patriarchal covenant, and that believers are grafted into Israel's covenant life. [Background] American Bible teacher (d. 2011) known for studies of the Jewish background of Jesus.
- Jeremiah: Yahweh called Israel a green olive tree, then kindled fire on it (Jeremiah 11:16). [Background] Prophet in Judah before the exile (Jeremiah 1:1-3).
- David and Goliath: Israel feared Goliath's appearance; David came 'in the name of Yahweh of hosts' (1 Samuel 17). [Background] An example of promises versus appearances.
- The Pharisees: They saw Sabbath-breakers; the Lord of the Sabbath was there (Matthew 12). [Background] 'For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath' (Matthew 12:8).

## Places [Background]
- Jerusalem (Zion) (named in the video): 'The Deliverer will come from Zion' (11:26).
- Hebron: Where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were buried (Genesis 49:29-31); the patriarchs are the root.
- Valley of Elah: David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17:2).
- Rome (named in the video): Gentile-background believers warned not to boast.
- Corinth: Where Paul probably wrote Romans.

## Key terms
- Qal vahomer: Arguing from the lesser to the greater ('how much more'), used four times in 11:12-24.
- First fruits: The first portion offered to God, consecrating the whole (Numbers 15:18-21; Romans 11:16).
- Olive tree: In the video, God's historical covenant people, rooted in the patriarchs.
- Mystery: Something once hidden, now revealed: the partial hardening of Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles (11:25).
- Chiasm: An inverted, mirrored structure (A B B' A'). The video prefers 'inversion and mirroring' because scholars debate chiasms here.
- Doxology: A hymn of praise to God's glory (11:33-36).
- Commonwealth of Israel: Pryor's phrase, echoing Ephesians 2:12 (LSB 'citizenship of Israel'): Gentile believers share Israel's covenant life.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Olive trees and grafting: Olive trees were among the most important crops of the land (Deuteronomy 8:8). Growers normally graft a cultivated shoot onto a wild stock; Paul pictures the reverse, a wild shoot grafted into a cultivated tree, which he himself calls 'contrary to nature' (11:24).
- The contribution of dough: Numbers 15:17-21 commands a cake from the first of the dough to be given to Yahweh throughout Israel's generations. The first portion offered to God marked the whole as belonging to Him.
- Romans 9-11 as a unit: The three chapters open with Paul's grief over Israel (9:1-5) and close with praise (11:33-36). The video sees the whole section as a defense of God's covenant faithfulness, ending in doxology.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Who is the root? (11:16) The patriarchs (the video, with Pryor; Chrysostom), the Messiah, God himself, or the first Jewish Christians. The video sets out all four before choosing the patriarchal covenant.
- Who is 'all Israel'? (11:26) A future large-scale turning of ethnic Israel (the video's view), the full number of the elect remnant through history, or the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile. The pronouns in 11:28 are central to the video's argument.
- Is there a chiasm? Some scholars find chiastic structures in Romans 9-11; others doubt them. The video speaks of inversion, mirroring and parallelism instead.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video lists Psalm 52:8 among places 'where Israel is actually like literally called an olive tree'; there the psalmist says 'as for me, I am like a green olive tree.' Jeremiah 11:16 and Hosea 14:6 do picture Israel.
- The video introduces the 'mystery' as 'verse 26'; the warning and the mystery are 11:25, and 'all Israel will be saved' is 11:26.
- The captions spell the scholar 'Dwight Prior' and the argument 'kalva'; the name is Dwight Pryor and the term is qal vahomer.
- The video's Jeremiah 11:16 adds 'The Lord of Hosts, who planted you, has decreed disaster against you'; that is Jeremiah 11:17.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why does it matter whether the olive tree is 'the church' or God's covenant people through history?
2. What does 'do not be haughty, but fear' (11:20) look like in practice?
3. How can unbelieving Israel be both 'enemies' and 'beloved' (11:28)?
4. Where are you reading the present moment by appearances rather than by God's promises?
5. Which line of the doxology (11:33-36) do you need to pray this week?

## Application
- (video) How often do we read the present moment by what we see rather than by what God has promised? The Pharisees saw Sabbath-breakers; the Lord of the Sabbath stood before them (Matthew 12). Israel feared Goliath's appearance; David came in the name of Yahweh of hosts (1 Samuel 17). The cross looked like the defeat of a blasphemous rabbi. The teacher urges reading three books well: God's word, reality and mankind, interpreting the last two through the first. A dream that sent him to God's word led his family into a painful wilderness season, and Wise Disciple emerged; this channel, Every Word, began from Jesus' answer to the devil in Matthew 4, quoting Deuteronomy 8:3.
